# Sirach Chapter 5 — The EMET Bible (Literal)

**Translator:** EMET | **Source:** Codex Vaticanus, Sirach 5 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-DC/SIR_005_page_001.jpg

---

**5:1** Do not set your heart on your wealth, and do not say, "It is sufficient for me."

**5:2** Do not follow your inclination and your strength in pursuing the desires of your heart.

**5:3** Do not say, "Who will have power over me?" — for the Lord will indeed exact retribution.

**5:4** Do not say, "I have sinned, and what has happened to me?" — for the Lord is slow to anger.

**5:5** Do not be so confident in atonement that you add sin upon sin.

**5:6** And do not say, "His compassion is great, and he will forgive the multitude of my sins" — for both mercy and wrath are with him, and his anger rests upon sinners.

**5:7** Do not delay turning back to the Lord, and do not put it off from day to day; for suddenly the wrath of the Lord will go forth, and at the time of vengeance you will perish.

**5:8** Do not set your heart on unrighteous wealth, for it will not benefit you in the day of calamity.

**5:9** Do not winnow in every wind, nor walk in every road — for that is the way of the double-tongued sinner.

**5:10** Be steadfast in your understanding, and let your word be consistent.

**5:11** Be swift to hear, and answer with patience; if you have understanding, give an answer to your neighbor; but if not, put your hand over your mouth.

**5:12** Honor and dishonor come from speaking, and a person's tongue can be his downfall.

**5:13** Do not be called a gossip, and do not lie in wait with your tongue; for shame belongs to the thief, and severe condemnation belongs to the double-tongued.

**5:14** In great and small matters, do no wrong, and do not become an enemy instead of a friend.

**5:15** Do not get a bad name — for shame is not the better part — and let not your tongue be your downfall.

---

*Translator's Note: This chapter is shorter in most manuscript traditions. The Hebrew (Cairo Genizah MS A) is partially extant. Greek is close to the Hebrew. The theme is two-fold: (1) presuming on God's patience (vv.1-8) and (2) the dangers of the double tongue (vv.9-15). "Double-tongued" renders Greek diglōssos = "two-tongued."*
